questions.q: A writer's scene has two old friends chatting pleasantly over coffee for three pages. What would Sorkin ask first?
choices: What value changes charge between the start and the end?
What does each of them want right now, and what's in the way?
Where is the hero's save-the-cat moment?
Which of the thirty-six dramatic situations is this?
questions.explain: Sorkin's test is intention and obstacle: without a want and something blocking it, the scene is just talk. The value-charge question is McKee's.

questions.q: In Sorkin's terms, what is a 'tactic'?
choices: The character's backstory wound
A plot point that spins the story in a new direction
What a character does to get past the obstacle
A line of subtext the character avoids saying
questions.explain: Tactics are the moves a character makes to get what they want; Sorkin says the tactics are the story.

questions.q: Sorkin credits Aristotle's Poetics as the source of his rules. What's the important caveat?
choices: Aristotle never discussed drama
Aristotle insisted every play have five acts
Sorkin has said he's never read the Poetics
The phrase 'intention and obstacle' is Sorkin's shorthand, not Aristotle's wording
questions.explain: Sorkin calls the Poetics the rule book, but 'intention and obstacle' is his own phrasing, close to acting-class language about objectives.

questions.q: In the courtroom climax of A Few Good Men, Kaffee has no proof that Jessup gave the order. What does he do?
choices: He goads Jessup, betting that pride will beat caution, until Jessup admits it
He produces a surprise witness who saw the order given
He reads Jessup's written order into the record
He drops the case and accepts a plea
questions.explain: Kaffee switches from polite questioning to provocation, a riskier tactic that breaks the obstacle when Jessup's contempt boils over.

questions.q: How does a walk and talk serve intention and obstacle?
choices: It hides the actors' faces so the dialogue carries the scene
It replaces conflict with movement
The destination works as a deadline, so the characters must win before they arrive
It lets the camera show the characters' backstory
questions.explain: Moving toward a destination adds a clock: each character has until the end of the corridor to get what they want.

questions.q: Why does The Social Network keep cutting back to two deposition rooms?
choices: To give a sprawling true story a clear frame of opposing sides who must answer
To satisfy the studio's lawyers
To show the story in strict chronological order
To create a dream sequence
questions.explain: The depositions bring the courtroom, Sorkin's favorite intention-and-obstacle machine, into a scattered story.

questions.q: A journalist admires Sorkin and wants to apply his method to a narrative feature. What should she borrow, and what shouldn't she?
choices: Borrow his rhythm; invent dialogue where the record is thin
Borrow nothing: drama and journalism have no overlap
Borrow the walk and talk by staging scenes with sources
Borrow intention and obstacle to find the story's engine; don't borrow his licence to invent
questions.explain: Every source wants something and meets resistance, which drives a narrative. But Sorkin openly favors story over the record, which no reporter can do.

questions.q: Which criticism is most often made of Sorkin's dialogue?
choices: It's too slow and full of pauses
It's mostly improvised by actors
Every character sounds like Sorkin, and they make speeches
It avoids conflict
questions.explain: Critics complain of one shared, articulate voice and of set-piece speeches; fans have even made videos of his recurring lines.

ideas: Somebody wants something, and something stands in the way: that's the drive shaft of every scene.
A character's tactics for getting past the obstacle are the story.
Put a destination at the end of the corridor, and a talky scene gets a deadline.
Wrap a scattered true story in two deposition rooms, so every flashback is evidence in a contest.
